  

## 2.3 The precision frame for the model and its derivation on the discontinuity principle

  

Every measuring instrument has, by design, specified a maximum degree of precision that can be obtained when using it. With this precision degree the precision degree allowed by the model of a given object should not be confused. It is a fact that the precision of measuring instruments is related to that of the model to which the measurement results are directed, and when the precision of the instrument challenges the model, its credibility can go into crisis, as has been well noted by Kuhn (1979 The essential tension, el capítulo sobre medición). In any case, the measuring instrument must have a sufficient precision according to the precision required by the object model. Each model implies by design an upper and lower limit for the dimensioning of its target, such that outside the limits the same is no longer measured (Tal 2012). In the case of numerical models, the required precision is usually also suggested numerically; in other cases the precision is made explicit only when necessary.

Too much lack of precision makes the model stop being useful, but too much precision also does. Consider the example of measuring the coastal distance of a city by the sea (Weisstein 2008, Mandelbrot 1982). Due to the fractal nature of the coastline, the greater the precision in its measurement, the resulting distance will extend more and more until ridiculous extremes, so the model in question (for instance a map) must be designed, among many other things, considering an specification of the maximum precision point to measure the coastal distance —of course one that does not cover the effect of the waves and the tide on the coast. This is not an isolated example, a maximum limit for forming a precision frame is a constant for all models, and just as it is a common idea that everything qualitative, by being numerically framed, becomes quantitative, it must be considered with equal attention the fact that everything quantitative, when transcending its own frameworks (and it always have them), produces a qualitative leap.

Also consider the example of planetary models, and the maximum precision they impose on their design. It can be broken with the extreme simplification of taking each body as a geometric sphere and considering, for greater precision in the analysis of the case, the deformations of each one in particular with respect to a perfect sphericity, and even up to uneven terrain (such as large mountains) in a certain area of ​​its surface... but to what extent? Is it useful for the planetary model to consider the influence of the distribution of innumerable small rocks to calculate the trajectory of a certain planet around its star? Such a distribution may well serve in another model that deals with the specific properties of the planet's surface, and although both models represent the same planet, they should be considered non-continuous. This might be recognized as the "discontinuity principle" between models that share the same target and is a direct consequence of the precision frame that models always have by design.

The discontinuity principle imposes a self-limitation of models, and it is previous or a priory respect to the technologically-conditioned precision of the measuring instruments that are each time coordinated with such models. For the same can be concluded when it comes to direct observation: it is possible to make a model (it does not matter at this point whether it is scientific or not) of the shape of a mountain, when appreciated from a certain distance, in relation to the rest of the landscape the mountain is part of, and one very different model when being placed on such mountain, for example representing its typical flora. Both models will result in different "gestalts" of the same target, and could never continue each other. What would it be like to continue them? Would it be like beginning a drawing at a distance, continuing it as one approaches the mountain, and concluding it when one is on the mountain itself? It would be as much as drawing trees on a planisphere in the Amazon area pretending to complete it.

That two models cannot continue each other does not mean that they cannot communicate with each other: the unitary structure that is proper to science allows unitary elements to be made up of unitary elements, and this is what happens with models that are said to represent the same target: one is considered a structural part of the other. Thus, the pattern of one model on the surface of a planet is part of the planet that revolves around the sun as a conceptual unity in the other model. Similarly, the pattern of a model of a cell of a species of tree is considered a constituent part of the conceptual unity "cell", which in the pattern of a model of the tree can be only an element without much relevance. This kind of fractality that is characteristic of the conceptual unitary structure of science allows that two or more models that have the same target but not superimposed precision frames are both appropriate, although incommensurable.

  

Acá puede haber un error de concepto. No es que los modelos sean inconmensurables por sus patrones; al contrario, la intersección en parte de sus patrones es lo que los hace conmensurables justamente. Son los elementos anexos, su materialidad, lo que los distingue e identifica como modelos distintos.


# 3. Ontology and epistemology of the target as an empirical differentiator of science

## 3.1 First approach to the relationship between world and nature from a review of what is understood by nature

  

So far nothing has been said about the target except that it is a kind of system to which the model points within a scientific representation, and that somehow contains a formal element, the pattern, homologous to the respective model pattern. In case it can be granted for now that this is so, is the pattern in the target real? Is the relationship between the pattern and the target similar to that of the pattern and the model? Can any "portion" of the world or nature be liable to become a model's target? Again: is it possible to find a pattern for anything belonging to nature or the world? When something in the world is finally categorized into these unities of knowledge called concepts, that is, after going through a conceptualization process, is it still the same thing? What do we mean by “world” and by “nature”, in any case, such that part of them or something into them, or even themselves can presumably become the object of a scientific model?

Perhaps the reader agrees that in a first, to say a pre-analytical impression, the meaning of the term nature today seems to contain the knowledge established and recognized as scientific, while the term world can refer to the scope of everything known in general, including non-scientific knowledge, such as religious, artistic, social-political, etc, and even a pre-institutional or daily knowledge. If there was an agreement on this, is it necessary to state that nature and the world are two different "things"? Or that they mean the same but from different conceptual frameworks (namely, scientific Vs. not-necessarily scientific)? In any case, would an account that includes both in their difference be permissible? And if possible, is there any advantage to our understanding of science in targeting this distinction?

The very question about the difference between nature and the world seems to challenge, or at least generate a tension, with the naturalistic position, which in general affirm that there is nothing that resists being apprehended by science. Put the other way round, naturalism maintains that if something can be thought of that cannot be scientifically explained, such a thing is not real, or it is an imaginary invention or simply an error. If it is granted the strong naturalistic position that reality is exhausted by nature, there does not seem to be room to speak of the world as if it were something else that nature cannot achieve. But which is the concept of nature underlined by the naturalistic position of science in current accounts? Throughout history there have been many markedly different conceptions of nature, quite discordant with each other, and in each case it can be verified that the meaning given to the term depends on what it is contrasted with in each case. Next is suggested a rough list to highlight five of the main cases in which it can be noticed how each sense of nature carries with it a demarcation criterion for natural knowledge. The list is not intended to be representative of the term's multivocality; simply serve as a platform to suitable develop the theses of this section.

i) Nature(φύσις)  Vs. convention (or law, νόμος). Contrasting the natural with the cultural is a topic since Plato and the Sophists. Here nature has the sense of what occurs regardless of human purposes. For many centuries science assumed the semantic weight of this meaning, since the knowledge it claimed was about things as they are, which in this case means: prior to being modified by the human gaze. So naive, such a look of nature has been heavily criticized in the last century with the consideration that all access to things is always "loaded" with preconceptions, including theoretical.

ii) Nature (φύσις) Vs. artifice (τέχνη). Similar to the previous one, nature denotes the kingdom of all that has not been modified by the human, in this case it is about a tangible modification of the object. Here nature is the set of all those things that have not been changed by technique or technology (cf. Aristotle, Phys., II, 192 b, 18 for an early formulation of this distinction). Those things certainly still exist on Earth, for example in pristine jungles. Perhaps it is even possible to agree that it can still be scientifically known without being modified in its natural state. The question is whether something whose knowledge has been accessed with the help of artificial means can be considered natural in this sense, even without being modified in its natural dynamics, for example an in vivo mammal cell observed under a microscope. This topic will be further discussed in section 4.5 below. For now, it can be said that if observation is loaded with theory, understood not only as a theory that interprets and knows things, but also as a theory that modifies things, then, if indeed science and technology are essentially combined, as will be argued in section 4, the natural / artificial distinction suffers the same fate as the natural / conventional distinction of item i.

iii) Nature Vs. God. This meaning of nature as creature or “the created” ruled strongly during the Middle Ages. Here the meaning of nature takes a turn with respect to items i and ii in the sense that it is no longer something that simply happens (the prefix φύ- in φύσις means “that which emerges by itself”) in contrast to what “is happened” thanks to something else (said in general, conventions and artifacts occur thanks to the human projects). Instead, in this case is God “what” exist with independence of anything else and nature occurs thanks to “something” else —in this case God. Regardless of whether the efficient cause of nature is God or whatever else, the contrast with the previous versions of the natural is raised: on the one hand that which is independent of "external" intervention, on the other that which is given thanks to an intervention of any kind. It is of utmost importance for this section to visualize these extremes and understand the error of being posed in any of them, in order to start thinking a proposal that can get out of the dichotomy "immanent existence" / "transcendent existence", which does not mean to fall in a vacue midpoint that says nothing and simply takes refuge in a "deflated" place just to avoid being criticized.

iv) The natural Vs. the psychic. This distinction has its origin in the Cartesian distinction between res extensa and res cogitans, and was object of a remarkable debate in the middle 20th century (cf. Murphy 1945, Kim 2003) when the possibility of breaking it began to be considered, that is, considering whether natural (scientific) knowledge is able to encompass the scope of the psychic. This topic will be further discussed below in section 3.2. 

v) The natural Vs. the supernatural. This distinction is the one with the greatest force in the philosophy of science debates of the last decades, to the point that even the historical reviews of the demarcation in science sound convincing when performed with this key, and it has its raison d'être in the search to distinguish science from pseudoscience as a false, misleading and even dangerous knowledge. In every declaration of demarcation of this kind a Manichaean background can be noticed without much effort, but in this particular case the degree of moral rift and elitist claims that it supposes and advocates is embarrassing.

Insofar as the term naturalism expresses the yearning and even the effort to reach knowledge through the scientific method in areas where the scientific knowledge has not arrived yet, for example, the Human Spirit sciences (Murphy 1945, Kim 2003), one may not be a naturalist as long as one does not share this aim, but it is difficult to think of a non-naturalist who denounces the error of a search posed in such terms. If now the bet is redoubled and what is intended with naturalism is to cover, not other areas of knowledge, but all areas of knowledge, at least as a possibility, and hence naturalism becomes “the wholehearted acceptance of scientific method as the only reliable way of reaching truths about the world of nature, society, and man” (Murphy 1945), then it is no longer lawful to see as senseless the one who moves away from this premise. At least there exist conditions for a debate. 

If one agrees with the naturalist's proposal that there is nothing (as a possibility) that escapes an objective reading and scientific presumption, it is worth asking what happens to other possible ways of understanding the world and the things of the world. If the extension of the scientific becomes absolute, does it not immediately become exclusive as well? The answer is no, but neither should one rush to settle a resounding "no". It is true that the scientific knowledge of whatever does not disqualify knowing the same thing or things from another non-scientific, for example artistic, religious, etc. framework. It follows from this simple fact that a scientific framework can well encompass everything without the need to deny extra-scientific knowledge. There is just a small caveat to be drawn from this: perhaps it can not be an issue of law, for example a logical deduction, that other kinds of knowledge are very often too hidden behind scientific knowledge, but is a historical issue, perhaps of a sociological character. Then science itself is forced to observe its effects from a non-scientific path; science is the one that must set its own limits.

According to this, even when some form of naturalism can be acknowledged since there is in principle anything that cannot be known in scientific terms, it is also true that formalized language of science cannot encompass the richness of vernacular language, which transcends it, even when recognizing that science contains an ordinary language that has been just partially technified. In consequence, it is worth reviewing what it means that something can be scientifically known and at the same time it is known in a non-scientific framework; if one can speak of the same thing or in what sense “that” is understood as different things. It is in these terms that it is desired to propose in this section the terminological distinction between world and nature, the first encompassing the totality of what is known beyond science, and the latter encompassing the entirety of scientific knowledge. It is not, as it could be understood, two spheres that complement each other and could for example be represented with diagrams, but two ambits of knowledge, two categories, which are related as far as they refer to the same things, just that in a different way. Consequently, it is a matter now of focusing on understanding the relationship between world (the non-scientific) and nature (the scientific), since it seems that in this relationship a clue can be found to clarify much of what has been said about the demarcation problem in science.

A suitable starting point to begin to understand the relationship between nature and world may be from the classical distinction between episteme and doxa, being the former part of academic knowledge, while the latest refers to the knowledge of those who have not accessed a certain context that offers a special education. Contrasting epistemic knowledge with opinion is not the same as contrasting it with the quackery that is presumed competent to give qualified opinions, as Plato often did when referred to the Sophists. Sophism, in current terms, is rather assimilable to pseudoscience. It is the place not to be reached (as Hansson 2009, 240 makes it clear); doxa, on the contrary, is the starting point to be left behind on the path of formation.

Similarly, if nature is presented as a synonym of essence, then essence may be understood as the element that makes daily language rise above itself for the first time to achieve something like universality—said in the terms that are being used in this study, becoming a concept, reaching a certain specificity to be part of a structural object.

  
  

## 3.2 Brief discussion against physical materialism and some comments on truth and reality

  

Most authors seem to agree that naturalism is somewhat less naive than materialism since it concedes the existence of non-material entities, understood here “matter” from classical physics, not from Aristotelian physics as in section 2 it has been done. Naturalists just deny that these non-material entities have their own realization or that they depend on something other than the material (Nagel 1956, p. 7). Now, if science is only able to know material forms and their realizations and also a naturalist wants to evaluate the scientific with a scientific tone (Danto 1967, 488) this seems to bring a problem. As a naturalist will only evaluate a form of knowledge from the canons of scientific reasoning, he becomes incapable of valuing any form of non-scientific knowledge; therefore, he has no authority to disqualify it. He is thus obliged to confine himself in a cloister where it only can be known what he accepted, and forced by his method to deny the non-scientific at the same time as to ignore it. This, which thus described seems so improbable, is not the most usual thing in our days, where many philosophers simply assume themselves to be naturalists without believing that they need more arguments for this than their declaration? But defining naturalism from an already naturalistic position is at least a fallacy and leads to hopelessly tautological arguments. For example, the custom of opposing the supernatural to nature has turned out to be a bit misleading because it takes for granted the impossibility of accessing the supernatural, for it is out of the naturalist cloister, and thus leaves nature without margin with which to be defined or specified. Opposing the supernatural, often identified as deceptive and despised, often linked with immaterial spirits and souls, results in the comfort of contrasting a position with the worst of his otherness.

The mind / nature focus (see item iv in previous subsection) allows moving from the appeal to medieval monsters and dragons while going straight to the subject / object focus, a distinctive mark of modernity. In the relationship between the physical and the mental it is sought on the one hand to explain the mental with precepts that have historically served to explain the physical, and on the other to define the physical as the non-mental, with the strategy that the mind is just the non-physical. The problem with this is that it cannot be done without solving the former. If the mind cannot be explained in a reliable way, neither can the physical be delimited from the mental in a reliable way. And the truth is that today it has not yet transcended an explanation that frees us from thinking of the mind as something other than a chimera.

Despite everything said, if naturalism is susceptible to a complaint it is not from the demonstration of causal connections between the physical and the supernatural; such contrastation, would return that “supernatural” to something physical and naturalism would remain untouched; then its comparison with the supernatural is, once again, a misguided task. The true Achilles heel of naturalism is suggested to be seen in its clinging to the scientific conceptual system, not as the only valid one, but as a valid one. Again; It is not here a question of demonstrating the validity of another type of reasoning or belief, but of questioning that of physics: the myth of space-time-causation. This is certainly not the first time this is suggested, but its conclusion is perhaps original: that having buried naturalism as it is currently understood, physics will be redeemed and in general also the philosophy of science.

Let physical matter as a term proper to physics, without letting it transcend to the field of philosophy in the aim of explaining science in general. For this, an idea of matter as opposed to form, but also to the efficient cause and the final cause of that explained may be ultimately more convenient, as has been attempted in section 2. Then the pattern embedded in the target can be understood in a homologous way than the pattern embedded in the model that this target represents. Such a pattern is therefore the formal part of the target, which gives it a material support that, as with the model, does not need to share the pattern's universality characteristics. Therefore, just as the atomic model is far from being the model of a particular atom exclusively, and can be supported by a graph, a formula, a syntactic explanation, etc., in an homologous way, the structure of an atom such as this model manifests it can be found in multiple empirical objects. Representation in science, from this point of view, consists of a relationship between two material entities (the symbolic model and the empirical target) each with a respective formal system that tends to be identified in an isomorphic way, as it will be attempted to show below in section 6.

Despite the intimate connection observed between the conception of ​​nature in science and the problem of demarcation, and having being conceded also that the demarcation of science with respect to pseudoscience is erroneous as a claim, this reconsideration wave seems to reach with much greater slowness to physicalistic naturalism. Is it a rejection of the discussions of a metaphysical tone that makes so many authors assume this position, at least unreflective in public terms, in order to better dedicate themselves to other problems typical of the philosophy of science, as if the philosophy of science had to do with something else? A direct victim of this sinchado is the idea of ​​truth. If the limits of science are dissolved, then all claims to truth also seem to be dissolved—at least truth as opposed to falsehood (sophistry, pseudoscience). But this is not the case if an explicit or implicit physicalistic naturalism is maintained. And in all those cases where it seems that the fairly common factor is to assume both the demise of the demarcation plus physicalism at the same time, the idea of truth remains in a bipolar state in which it cannot be simply accepted but neither it is allowed to die.

Another victim is the very close idea of reality. In the multicolored variety of realisms that have arisen at this time this madness is evidenced. What idea of truth and what idea of reality is suggested that may fit with what is outlined in this essay? A truth and a reality not naturalistic in the sense of nature as opposed to falsehood and to the supernatural respectively, but pre-naturalistic in the sense of nature as contrasting to the world. It is the world, the non-scientific, the place of the real and the true, although both still irreflexive as such, which by specification science manages to make a unitary object. And so the reality and the true character of the scientific object are modified, only to the extent of its specification, as it will be seen hopefully clearer in the next subsections. If necessary, it can be called backward realism, by following Ratcliffe (2004) in their comments to Putnam. But how many philosophers of science are going to agree with the claim that reality is first of all what it is considered as such in everyday life, that is, among everything that is not scientifically proven?

All this invites to reflect that the inquiry about the reality of, say, H2O which we consider objective although we question its existence is not so relevant, nor the reality of the water we speak of when washing our hands, whose existence we do not question, although we do not consider it in objective terms. And that much more interesting to concentrate the research effort is the relationship between both, non-scientific water and scientific water, in order to finally be dismayed at the effectiveness of the verb “to be” saying, for centuries and absolutely effective, in any scientific context, that H2O “is” water.

  
  

## 3.3 The influence of the Democritean tradition and the Anaximandric tradition in western thought —including the scientific thought

  

Now, with full awareness that these topics are too important for the brief treatment that is being given in this work, whose main questions are certainly elsewhere, attention will only be drawn to a way of interpreting this issue in terms that in a one way or another, each time with their own features and in their context, there have accompanied the history of science and philosophy. It is about a contest regarding the search for truth that initially divided thinkers like Democritus and in some way Plato and Aristotle on the one hand and Anaximander, Empedocles and Heraclitus on the other. According to the first group (and once again the reader is asked for mercy for the child simplification with which this profound subject is being treated herein) the truth (and the real in a strong sense) resides in stable, eternal, universal, ideal, etc. conditions, and the tangible world, the world knowable by mortals, is a corrupted derivation of that sphere from which it falls figuratively but also ontologically. Thus, the truth to which the human accesses is partial and knowledge as an act is a movement (perhaps asymptotic) towards that which is perfect and immutable, which is thus established as a beginning (arkhé) and as an end (télos). The Cartesian tradition, whose influence is perhaps still the majority today in the philosophy of science, seems to be much closer to this “top-down” view and that is why the discussions on realism hover around questions such as to what extent the real can be accessed, or why such a goal cannot be accomplished. An extreme skepticism or anti-realism in this sense also falls on this side because they must assume the same point of view of the position that they deny.

For the other side of thinkers, that have had participants in history such as Hume and Nietzsche, the truth that man can access is the consequence of an emergency from chaos, the result of the configuration at first randomly from the unconfigured. Notably, this “chaos” can be as difficult to justify metaphysically as the “ideal” for the former authors. For both sides, télos can be thought to be roughly the same (objective knowledge), but here arkhé is, it can be said, opposite. Here there is no world of ideas from which the imperfect derives, but an Anaximander ápeiron from which what can be known arises. And therefore the idea of ​​truth as correspondence (homoíosis) is meaningless, since there is no ideal model from which to evaluate the false. Instead, the idea of ​​truth as unconcealment (alétheia) fits well. The truth in this sense is not understood in its contrast with its opposite, falsehood, but from the dynamic to unconcealment. All the philosophers of science who are recognized as pragmatists are much closer to this second sense of truth and from such a conception it is that they criticize the strong structuralist position—and this despite the fact that hardly anyone can argue that science lacks structure.

The present work intends to be inserted as well in the second, “bottom-up tradition", understanding everything known as unhidden (perhaps it is better understood as configured or assimilated from chaos or randomness), in a gradual process in which the movement towards configuration, assimilation or unhiding has been called specification (see section 1.4 above), and that scientific knowledge has greater specification in general with respect to everyday knowledge. It is worth clarifying again that in general all institutional knowledge is more specified and is more objective with respect to everyday knowledge; science also has a particular structure that allows it to be differentiated in some way from other non-scientific (objective) institutional knowledge (see section 1.2 above). As advanced in the introduction, there is no attempt here to understand the general question of the known out of chaos, but the movement from the everyday (just) known to the scientific known. For this reason it is framed as a philosophy of science and not of cognitive science, neuroscience or psychology study. This distinction is on the way a necessary antidote to the tendency to think that, like science, everyday thought also consists of representations, although no one has ever seen a model for it, and then one seeks, with very ingenious but unfounded inferences, equivalents devices to such a supposed model in a "inner world" or in neurons.

  
  

## 3.4 The world-nature tension and the daily anchor as a limit to the conjecture power of a hypothesis

  

Granting the terminological proposal that nature is the realm of the conceptual and the world that of the non-scientific, and considering that natural knowledge is a conceptualized derivative of pre-natural or worldly knowledge, so following the famous quote by Albert Einstein (1936) that “[t]he whole of science is nothing more than a refinement of everyday thinking”, the working premise to be defended now is that the world is turned into nature for the first time when a hypothesis on it is posted. This fact does not seem to require an intervention in the world. But immediately an observation (or in particular a measurement) must occur in order to test such a hypothesis. Before the respective observation, the hypothesis raises unitary elements in nature only potentially, such as a possibility. And it is through testing (in some cases called contrastation) that this possibility becomes a fact. So it is possible to make a hypothesis about the world without intervening on it, but it is not even possible to think of a model of the world without intervening on it. A hypothesis is thus a conjecture, a belief or presumption that has the effect of taking an element from the world and turning it to an unitary object. Therefore it is an indispensable element, and it could even be said it is the primary engine for the design of a model. This definition gives some light to the conceptualization process mentioned in section 1.3 when citing the Standard ISO 704. Such a conceptualization process is not without intercession in the world, but it begins with the hypothesis, which has such intercession as a possibility that takes place at the time of the test.

Hypothesizing about the world and observing it, the world is turned into nature, otherwise science cannot see anything (Duhem 1991, pp. 153-6; Carrier 2012, pp. 9-19; Teller 2013). Thus, the well-known warning that observation is theory-laden can be rethought by saying that observation is firstly hypothesis-laden, and a direct not too far-fetched corollary of it is that nature is a concept-laden world. According to this, one could ask how much, in what sense and to what extent the world is laden by a hypothesis to get natural knowledge. Although it is direct to agree that observation is hypothesis-laden, nobody would risk that observation is completely indebted by the hypothesis. Affirming that no aspect or degree of scientific observation is independent of the hypothesis from which the observation took place leads to a kind of tautological alley where anything that is asserted can be smoothly “observed” with only a consistent hypothesis in itself. If this is clearly not the case for science, then what is the limit in this "loading" of observation by the hypothesis? It is intuited by what has been said that the limit must be sought in the tension between nature and the world. If the hypothesis makes scientific knowledge emerge from non-scientific knowledge, then the limit to the hypothesis power can only be placed in something like a world's resistance to being conceptualized.

There is a well-established knowledge outside of the scientific knowledge; every scientist, needless to say, is also a human being who regardless of doing science knows that the stone is hard, water to be heated at a certain moment boils, fire is hot, the rain falls down, and so on, and all this can be expressed by the language beyond science. This daily knowledge, that can be more or less influenced by scientific theories in general, operates as an anchor for all novel proposals, which as a consequence cannot move too much away from such daily established knowledge. There is, if someone wants to see it this way, a semantic boundary or frame that the world imposes on the novel model, which has to do with the semantics of the terms that the model uses, including the terms naming the model: their title. There is a model that represents the respiratory system, then insofar as it has been confirmed the model "is" the respiratory system, and then, consequently, "there is" out-there a respiratory system as the model explains—but not perhaps in absence of the model. This is a kind of prescription from the model to turn something in the world into a natural system, although the model does not prescribe, for example, the meaning of “respire” and “system”, but it modifies them. Another model includes a wheel. The wheel implemented from the model is tied to the model´s wheel as from the word that names both, which is not a mere guttural "wheel" but the bridge from which it is possible to think in some way the difference between both the empirical and the symbolic wheel.

A new scientific insight (and this could be said as well for a philosophical or a theological insight) in general moves away from a common sense of what is regularly known about the world, but it cannot move too far from this pre-scientific anchor. If a model saying that stones can fall up became successful, it will be said that the scientist who published the model is extremely persuasive, and probably s/he will come to be considered a genius by posterity… But for all this, s/he must empirically demonstrate the meaning of her/his symbolic bet. On the one hand, there is like a system of relations at a certain radius around the pre-scientific world, and on the other hand the model must have the ability to attract towards itself this pre-scientific world, deforming in some way the perimeter of this daily knowledge, then s/he must convince other scientists, with all that this implies, and once the scientific community follows their principles, it is probably a matter of time that even in everyday life everybody comes to speak in terms of that model—although this latter has questionable relevance for the establishment of a scientific model.

This centripetal force that a model must own in order to be successful can also be read in methodological terms. The model moves away from common sense, but into its own canons it must arrive at successful experimental results and these successful experiments are required to be reproducible, this is, outside the laboratory, so that the model has a potential applicability—more precisely, so its applicability is not impossible. In this sense, that is, in the sense that the pre-theoretical world somehow is what conditions a scientific novel model, it can be said that an hypothesis and its resultant model are as well world-loaded, since at the time of conceiving a model in abstract terms it is possible to disdain the pre-scientific world, but at the moment of carrying an experiment out it is not longer possible, and that model, to have the ability to attract the pre-scientific world, must have the characteristic of being loaded in part by that world. A totally unworldly model is a schizophrenic attempt that will never have the right to transcend nor results useful for anyone.

In summary, the farther away an hypothesis is formulated from the pre-scientific world the more difficult it will be for it to come to transcend. However, to the extent that it actually transcends, the greater distance this model is conceived from the world previous to it, the higher the brilliance will be attached to it once the community declares it confirmed by experimental evidence. For this it is not possible to elicit a rule that is valid for all cases, since of all the unitary elements that the model presents as innovators (there can be conceded to always be a good part of other ones yet known before the proposal) usually only the confirmation of a few unitary elements is enough for the model to be considered acceptable, generally the most falsifiable ones. For the confirmation of the remaining ones until the model is free of mysteries science of course continues his normal work, already with the model consecrated, that is, among other things, conceded to the engineers.

  



# 4. Interaction between the scientific model and the measuring instrument in scientific and technological activity

### 4.1 Introduction to the problem of measurement in science through a representative example  

There does not seem to be much dissent between the different accounts as to what measurement is, generally defined as the process by which a number is attributed to an aspect (sometimes called quantity, sometimes called magnitude) of an object under measurement. The strategy of this section is to try to advance in defining not directly measurement but that technological instrument based on its characteristics by which it is generally said to be a measuring instrument. If this can be achieved, then the definition of measurement as an activity is straightforward: measurement is what the measuring instrument does, or what people do with it. The step from measurement as it will be specified below to the dimension (of non-numerical aspects of objects) could be carried out without major inconveniences.

The question about the measuring instrument comes up with the question about representation in science, which somehow involves the represented empirical end and the representative symbolic end. To properly understand the scientific model, it is essential to take into account both the empirical and the symbolic fields, but the relationship between them, the representation itself, is very difficult to reach if the analysis is limited to the scientific model, for a simple reason: the scientific model helps understand what it represents, but does not interact with it. In this sense, a scientific model cannot be properly considered an instrument. Technological instruments are in charge of modifying nature based on a pack of models, among which are undoubtedly scientific models, and on the other hand, the interaction with nature itself, not in order to modify it but to know it is carried out by the measuring instrument. Using the metaphor of a nervous system (NS), the models constitute the central NS of science, and as for the peripheral NS, the measuring instruments are the afferent NS and the technological instruments the efferent NS. A particular look at how this coordinated system works to give rise to both scientific and technological practice is what is intended to be shown in this section.

Every measuring instrument necessarily has an empirical ambit to be able to interact with what it measures, and a symbolic ambit to be able to interact with the models that take the data obtained in its interaction with the measured object, so that everything that has been said so far in the previous sections applies to measuring instruments, as these are models—although a very particular kind of models. This means a measuring instrument is both an instrument, if an instrument is defined as any object that is able to interact with other objects in empirical terms, and a model, taking the definition of model from section 2 where a scientific model, according to its final cause, is each unitary arrange from which it is possible to dimension an empirical target. The empirical target to be dimensioned is a quantity, and the unitary arrangement has to do with the numerical scale with which this measured quantity is set. Thus, in summary, a measuring instrument can be considered any instrument that is also a model, or any model that is also an instrument.

Everything that is said in this section about the measuring instrument can be easily extended for measuring systems, that is, systems in which various measuring instruments interact to obtain the value of a quantity.

There are two instances in which the empirical and the symbolic communicate, and that is where the attention will be focused to get as close as possible to the phenomenon of representation that will be properly studied in section 6. When the instrument interacts with the object to be measured and displays a data, which is usually numerical, there is an empirical-symbolic movement, after which the raw data thus obtained is processed to be finally attributed to the quantity of the object measured, in a symbolic-empirical movement. The names that are usually used for these movements are respectively reading and outcome. A little example will help clarify the picture so that I can better discuss these points of interest later.

The reciprocity between the empirical and the symbolic that make up the measuring instrument make both subject to each other, so that on the one hand the empirical design marks a basic path for the symbolic stages, but in turn the symbolic design can decide which empirical stages intermediates to consider as part of the process and which ones not.
