According to the diagrams obtained from the example, it can be seen that the empirical-symbolic movement occurs with Q1, the displacement L of the knob indicating the reading. Note how deeply it is necessary to specify the rawness of the data, so as to be able to understand how the empirical scope of the measuring instrument is able to be understood separately of its symbolic scope. The feasibility of this separation and the simplicity of the empirical-symbolic point connection allowed by it will take on a preponderant weight a little below when trying to answer some classic questions of measurement theory, and in general of scientific representation.

At the other end, the one of the symbolic-empirical movement, the same simplicity can hardly be reached. In general, the debates in measurement theory focus on the justification of this symbolic-empirical attribution: how the outcome obtained is to be applied to an empirical quantity; to what extent this attribution is lawful and how it should be understood. This is actually a variable of the so-called coordination problem: how is it possible to know if two different measuring systems or methods measure the same quantity? An early response to this problem was given by the so-called operationalist movement, which stated that the meaning of quantity-concepts is determined by the set of operations used for their measurement. According to this premise, different operations could be concluded to measure different quantities. [conventionalism, etc...] 

Now the reader is asked to note a detail concerning the use of the measuring instrument in its context in a scientific environment: that the outcome can never be applied to the empirical quantity if there is no model “in the middle” that explains the relationship between the quantity and the whole object. There are no measuring instruments that measure an objectless quantity. A mercury thermometer does not simply measure "temperature", so said is just an elision to mean that what it measures is actually the temperature of a given atmosphere, for example. The sun clock in antiquity measured the effects of the sun-cycle, only in this way could it be said to measure “time”. The question of how we have gone from measuring the duration of a phenomenon to simply measuring "time", or from measuring ambient temperature to measuring "temperature" is closely related to the standard unit, which will be analyzed in the next subsection.

In current measurement theory discussions, the object model is generally taken for granted to the point of becoming implicit, so to end consequently out of analysis. And yet the contemplation of the whole object model is essential to note that the outcome is never directly related to an empirical quantity (as shown by the yellow dotted arrow in the diagram). Instead, the outcome as a symbolic data is related to other symbolic data within the model, and then the whole object model is related to its respective target, thus attributing the measured value of the quantity, among other data. The semantics of quantity-terms is then understood from the semantics of the whole object, in the sense that they are not two problems, but one and the same: just as it is assumed that the attribution of the outcome to a measured quantity is a unitary point of the representation of an object, it must also be assumed that the representation of an object is not carried out in any other way but through the equalization of its unitary points, which becomes factual in the act of measurement —and for the first time in the experiment.

Esto no resuelve el problema de coordinación, sino que lo mueve hacia...

In sum, the strategy that has been adopted in this study to pose the coordination problem (not yet to start solving it) is to notice first of all that it is the object model, to which the measurement result is directed, what prescribes the identification of the measured quantity, not the measurement model directly, so it is not the measurement model which gives the objectivity to “that” measured. The outcome of the measurement is just a magnitude value, like a kantian “phenomenon”. Such objectivity is given by the whole object model, in which each magnitude value is the value “of” the empírical object. Thus the object model acts as the kantian “transcendental consciousness”. This shows that the problem of empirical-symbolic movement transcends the theory of measurement to the general problem of representation of the scientific model. The fact suggested in section 1.1 that the theory of measurement is an indispensable constituent part of the philosophy of science and that the act of measurement is an outstanding activity for the analysis of scientific representation suggests that affirming that the status of the outcome of measurement must be evaluated through the complete object model, far from leaving out the debates of this type that take place in the area of measurement theory, these become of utmost importance for the philosophy of science and for the clarification of representation in the scientific model.

To begin to outline an answer, it will be assumed as the work thesis that the objectivity of the symbolic-empirical leap on which the clarification of the representation in science depends is given by the empirical-symbolic leap on the other end of the measuring instrument according to the scheme suggested. The measuring instrument has the function of "reducing" the measured object to a quantity, through the steps that are necessary, each one supervised by a respective parallel symbolic step, and at the end of this reduction the empirical-symbolic connection applies, which the measurement model itself (its symbolic dimension) guarantees that it is equivalent to the outcome, that is, to the measured quantity of the object. With this, the problem or representation nor the coordination problem have not been solved, but have been greatly simplified by moving them both at once towards the single end of the measuring instrument: the reading.

  
  

## 4.2 The unitary element recognized as standard unity supports any measurement process


According to what the example in the previous subsection shows, it does not seem like much can be gained from the simplicity of reading. This is a certainly controversial operating point in which a number is assigned to the knob displacement. The move from the knob displacement (empirical) to the number (symbolic) seems to be totally unproblematic, at least it is in practice. And will not this simplicity be the relevant and the most important detail to be evaluated? Is not the measuring instrument lead in each case to disarticulate the complexity of the measured object to steal only one aspect of it, a quantity—said in terms that are being used here: a unity? Thus thought, the measuring instrument is a "delator" of unitary elements in the measured object, and it does so by simplifying the empirical perception of this object in stages, until it is reduced to the unity it needs. Once this unity (Q1) is obtained free of all context (this is the condition for specification of a concept as seen in section 1.4), getting the number that represents it seems to be an obvious step. But it only seems so.

The tip of the knob is displaced on a graduated background whose successive points or lines are labeled from zero to the maximum amount the instrument is by design able to measure. The units of the corresponding numbers indicate that in general what they mark is not the distance the knob tip moves but directly the temperature. This is because the calculation corresponding to the successive symbolic steps for each temperature reading, or correspondingly for each potential knob displacement, is already implicit in the labeling of such graduation. Therefore the data of interest here, the distance of the knob displacement that corresponds to the crudest data, is hidden at least in practice. Highlighting it at this moment is necessary to expose what is being sought, the empirical-symbolic movement in its most naked state.

But what is the implicit complexity in saying, when the cursor is displaced with respect to its initial point, that the movement has been x millimeters? The complexity is a little more notable in the scale by which the displacement corresponds to x millimeters—although in general an overlooked complexity in practice. The scale is associated in all cases with a standard unit, and the determination of such a unit (for instance the second for the unit of time) is today a highly complex question, in high contrast to what is known to have occurred some centuries ago and from the prehistoric beginning of the measurement, when the unit was simply determined by an imposition that had to be followed. In the case in which the unit is thus determined, for example when in the old days the grain of wheat was taken as the unit of weight, it can be seen how this standard unit was the first nuclear unitary element in which subsequent scientific knowledge would then gradually be built. The standard unit as it is calculated nowadays, namely from iterative calculations between several crossed instruments, even though it is much many times more precise, has no theoretical endorsement to be taken as the unitary element in which scientific knowledge is in general posed, except by forgetting or deliberately omitting the process of its establishment, which shows that it is in no way a starting point for the establishment of anything. However, as much as it is no longer supported by arbitrary imposition but by a complex system of cross-instruments, it is still true that it is a convention, only now perhaps more reliable and precise. And it is this convention by which an empirical unity equals a symbolic unit that operates today and has always operated as the foundation of the representation of the scientific model through the measuring instrument, at least in the area of the physical sciences. For the very meaning of the existence of the standard unit today is still the same: to be the unitary element of universal reference.

The definition of the measurement standard as the universal unitary reference element triggers a fractal succession of topics most of which cannot be addressed herein, since the scope of this section is delimited according to the following two criteria: to support from a measurement point of view what has been said in the previous sections about the unitary elements, and on the other hand give way to the discussion on representation in science of section 6. And according to this it can be seen that the problem of the symbolic-empirical movement that had been limited to the scientific representation itself, can now be treated again from the solution obtained in the analysis of the empirical-symbolic movement, which is characteristic of the theory of measurement: what supports the attribution of a symbolic quantity to the empirical object that has been measured is the standard unit. Thus, what justifies that it is finally said that the temperature of the measured object has increased by 8,84 ºC is the simple transfer whereby a movement in the cursor is assumed to correspond to 36 millimeters, plus a combo of successive calculations that belong to the measurement model, which depend on the measuring instrument in each case and in this section will not be questioned since do not imply a movement between the empirical and the symbolic. And to be able to say that a movement in the cursor is assumed to correspond to 36 millimeters it is necessary a standard unit to be established, from which it can be known what 36 millimeters means.

  
  

## 4.3 The standard unity as the key to assess the objectivity of a measurement model

  
Hermann von Helmholtz was the first to explicitly outline the attribution problem: “[W]hat is the objective meaning of expressing through denominate numbers the relations of real objects as magnitudes, and under what conditions can we do this?” (1887: 4). In view of what has been said so far, it can be answered that the objective meaning of associating certain empirical quantities with numbers is the equivalence relation between the respective patterns, which is guided by the standard unit and consummated in the act of measurement. Numbers are adequate for expressing a quantity insofar as such quantity can be compared to a standard that gives it a magnitude from its multiple.

The ability to refer everything numerical associated with a magnitude to only one representative element of such magnitude (the standard unit) and that the one-to-one relation in the empirical-symbolic game of such standard unit is sufficient as a guarantee to associate to any other number related to the same magnitude: that is perhaps the point of advantage in terms of conceptual and specification capacity that the numerical sciences have over the non-numeric sciences. But this does not mean that the lack of numbers condemns a science to the lack of objectivity, since objectivity is generally related to the specificity with which the unitary elements of a model are defined, and these elements can reach a sufficient specification without being epistemically associated with numbers, as many examples from the biological sciences demonstrate.

A classic question in measurement theory is why some attributes are measurable and others are not. The discussion surrounding this question has a particular interest in the social sciences, whose scientific character is often questioned based on the respective questioning of its ability to measure what it works with, assuming that of the physical sciences as a criterion for how measurement should be understood. Within this framework, the present proposal can advance in a kind of resolution saying that anything, although not numerical, is dimensionable (if it is numerical, this means measurable) insofar as it is made up of unitary elements, and it is so as much as specified are its unitary elements. This seems to allow a prudent and honest working criterion for evaluating measurement or dimensioning in the social sciences, according to which in each case they must ask: how specific is the unity we have defined as dimension standard? There are no yes/no-answers here, and the dimensioning that starts from a more precise and reliable unity will be considered respectively more accurate and reliable.

The distinction between qualitative and quantitative thus takes on a new light, although for sure not enough to give an end to the current debates, but it may help to see as qualitative magnitudes those that, being defined by degrees by the daily language, a standard unity specific enough to serve as the basis for a quantitative scale has not been found for them. The immediate question, which will only be posted here, arises as to whether all the magnitudes that today are known as qualitative are also potentially quantitative or if there is any additional factor that shows that certain magnitudes can never, in principle, become quantitative.

In section 1 it has been noted that a concept is formed from its usual meaning, gradually losing its relationship with random factors, generally with its background, until reaching the maximum point of being related only to other concepts in a self-sufficient network, clarifying that such an extreme can never be reached, but that is what science tends to achieve in his endless activity. As the standard is indeed a unitary element, then its specification will depend on how much it can be emancipated from its context, in particular from emerging factors that modify it randomly; to put it another way, its specification will depend on its ceteris paribusness. This condition is extremely difficult to achieve in some cases, for example for the alleged measurements in psychology, where the variation in responses due to countless and unrecognizable factors of human psychology—because they usually depend on the unending history of the individual surveyed—is hardly remedied with long statistical strips. This does not detract from the scientific character of the dimensioning process, but in any case it must be strongly considered that the confidence in the results obtained is directly proportional to the specification accomplished of the standard unity chosen for such dimensioning.

  
  

## 4.4 On Euclid's Elements as the usual first-milestone for measurement theory histories

  

The question of why the measurement theory has not given the importance it deserves to the standard unit as an epistemological articulator for a multiplicity of other relevant concepts, in particular for the crucial relationship between the empirical and the symbolic, has at least two answers. One has to do with the complexity that is observed today around the definition of a standard unit, which has encouraged theorists to move away from the idea that it is a simple element from which to explain other elements; rather, the standard unit needs a multiplicity of other elements to be explained. These considerations do justice to the pragmatic aspect of the standard, but also to a series of epistemic aspects, such as ... that would be lost if the unit is considered as an element without intrinsic complexity. Therefore, it should not be interpreted that such claim is part of the present proposal, which tries to emphasize that nevertheless, even with the capital complexity presented by the establishment of the standard unit, its very meaning as a standard unit consists in operating as a reference, and if this were not so, it would lose all its value. The issue of interest then is in any case why, despite its lack of simplicity, in the world of measurements it is still necessary to establish, for each magnitude, a standard unit. The standard unit as a reference is essential, because it is not just a point from which to mark a distance from other points. It is rather an empirical-symbolic reference; the establishment of the standard, as complex as it may be, means: this (empirical) object is equivalent to (symbolic) unity; in formula it could be set as oneemp ≡ onesym. Even though in the context of metrology the lack of its absolute character is notable due to the iterative nature of the network of measurement systems that define it, outside the context of metrology scientists and engineers assume and can trust the formula oneemp ≡ onesym, and that is ultimately the main value that makes the existence and persistence of the standard.

The second reason for the theoretical deflation of the standard could have to do, in the author's opinion, with the reference to some passages of Euclid which is traditionally referred to as something like the beginning of thinking about measurement. The first two definitions in book V are cited in particular:

Def. V.1. A less magnitude is said to be a part of a greater magnitude, when the less measures the greater; that is, when the less is contained a certain number of times exactly in the greater.

Def. V.2. A greater magnitude is said to be a multiple of a less, when the greater is measured by the less; that is, when the greater contains the less a certain number of times exactly.

The first impression these quotes suggest is that at the beginning of measurement thinking there was no reference to a unit. And indeed it is not easy to find the attribution of any importance to unity in later theories of measurement. Without the space to carry out a comprehensive demonstration, the purpose of this section is to draw attention to this inconvenient reading, which in fact is found in contemporary theorists and not in Euclid, who in turn did make an Empirical / Symbolic reference in book VII of the same treatise.

Def. VII.1. A unit is that by virtue of which each of the things that exist is called one.

Def. VII. 2. A number is a plurality made up of units.

Def. VII.3. A number is part of a number, the smallest of the largest, when it measures the largest.

Note the similarity between Def. V.1 and Def. VII.3. Perhaps contemporary theorists have preferred to refer to Book V and not Book VII because this is known as an articulation of the Pythagorean tradition of geometry, in particular of his theory of ratio, and Euclid, who in his Elements performs a manifest overcoming of his previous theorists and establishes the bases of geometry for the posterity, concentrates in book V the principles of his new point of view. If this is so, or insofar as it is, it should be noted that Book VII may well be understood as containing elements proper to the Pythagorean tradition, but it will not for that reason have the defects of the formulations for which this tradition had been criticized.

It should also be noted that the first postulates of this book do have the empirical / symbolic reference that is sought to be highlighted here, as essential to measurement. The Def. VII.3 sets out how numbers are measured against each other based on which is the largest and which is the smallest. To know what a number is, the previous definition clarifies that a number “is a plurality made up of units”. Unity appears here, but in terms that are called symbolic in this study. So the Def. VII.1 which begins by relating the unit to “each of the things that exist” has been put before it. Here in Def. VII.1 is where Euclid manifests the oneemp ≡ onesym formula, which is the one that is proposed in this study to consider as the main and foundational for any possibility of measurement.

To all this it is convenient to clarify that, in his Def. VII.1 Euclid surely did not have the act of measurement in mind as such, and when he used the term "measurement" he did not refer primarily to measuring instruments. Instead, the oneemp ≡ onesym formula was of necessary formulation and definition for him because, being a student of Pythagoras, he must have assumed to some extent his ontological commitments, in particular the belief that mathematical relations were intrinsically linked to the things of the world. This empirical / symbolic conjugation, which also became part of the philosophers from Plato, did not lead the Greeks to include the instruments of measurement in the foundations of their theories—it is known how reluctant the elite (and therefore the thinkers) of this society was to manual activities; this happened, as it is well known, in the Renaissance, when there was a society that allowed the emergence of artisan-wise persons for the first time in the West.

For this reason (because the Greeks have been reluctant to think of the measuring instrument), this section concludes by suggesting not only that Book VII be considered in the history, albeit minimal, of measurement theory, but also consider abandoning the Euclid's comfortable point as the first birth of thought about measurement. Measuring instruments existed many centuries before Euclid, and consideration of what historical manifestations about them should be considered measurement theory or not is ultimately a matter of interpretation.

  
  

## 4.5 Difference between measurement and direct observation from their respective standard unities

  

Direct observation is a term usually found in the literature, which can be assumed to mean an observation without the aid of an instrument (Herman 1994); it is a kind of measurement with just the human body. The situation of a chemist measuring the concentration of a substance in a test tube by looking at the color of the liquid reflects a measurement in all its right, since relatively inaccurate being that the chemist can get more specific information about the concentration of the liquid by using other methods, for example through a measuring instrument like a colorimeter. In view of what has been said so far, the lack of precision and consequently of confidence in the result of such direct observation is directly associated with the absence of a sufficiently specific standard unit to which to refer the result of measurement. It is possible that a standard unity can be found, after all, as a color palette with which to subjectively contrast the color of the sample, but this has no comparison in terms of specification with the numerical standard that a colorimeter uses to obey its outcome.

Not for this fact direct observation ceases to be a way of measurement, although it is understood why in many cases science tends to a state where direct “qualitative” observation is replaced by more accurate “quantitative” measuring instruments. This is not to say that by quantifying something that was not quantifiable prior to its measurement knowledge becomes more scientific or in some sense better; just that science, historically, has leaned toward mathematics, and this means, it has tending to abolish direct observation by putting into play a measuring instrument each time the testing of a model has been carried out (Michell 2003; Kuhn 1961, section V). It is worth insisting that, if the advance of science has consisted of mathematization is not because “the world is written in a mathematical language”, but because physics, explicitly or implicitly assumed to be the paradigm of all sciences, is based on mathematics. If another science were able to settle with similar success in a different discipline, for example in the biology of the nervous system, it is thought that it might be possible to describe a (another) nature from eventualities of the nervous system of every living being. This may be the dream of (almost?) all neuroscientists.

In philosophy of science some terms are often called theoretical because they are unobservable, such as electrons, genes and gravitational forces (Friedman 2011; Carnap 1966, section 23). Not to be observable their analysis seems more problematic and their ontological status is discussed, this is, it is even discussed to what extent they can be said to be "real" and therefore in which extent they share the natural status with other terms that seem to lack this problem since they are directly observable. Nevertheless, in view of the distinction between nature and world done in section 3.1 it can be argued that all scientific terms are equally theoretical, not some over others, since they are part of nature. Added to this is what has just been said: that direct observation of natural objects is becoming less, and tends to stop being a criterion of assessment of the existence of whatever in science.

Consider a calculation-free estimation based on a self-experience case: a series of logs spanning both banks of a river support the human weight, and they do so because the repeated (science-free) experience has shown it. In some other place, an engineer calculates the materials needed for the construction of a bridge. There is an abyss between both cases. The bridge in the second case (and by no means in the former) is a physical-mathematical object, and indeed so are the people potentially walking over it, which, in turn, have a previously estimated weight. Then the bridge, like the people, are so theoretical constructs as the electron that cannot be directly-observed—since the fact of being unable of direct observation, as argued above, is finally irrelevant. Physics tends to increasingly ignore instrument-free observation and concentrate its foundation on mathematics with numbers derived from measurement. Under this glass, a measuring tape theoretically equates the latest accelerator for measuring the displacement of a subatomic particle, while this particle at its time theoretically equates the box measured by the tape. The box can certainly be perceived by sight, but this is finally inconsequential; what ultimately matters is the measurement outcome.

  
  

## 4.6 Description of a technological-scientific scheme to discuss the role of measurement in science

  

Next, it is intended to unravel step by step a particular view of the process involved in scientific and engineering practice, considering the main activities that are necessarily involved. According to the explanatory scheme adopted herein, it can be seen that the different activities fluctuate between the symbolic and the empirical, and also between the theoretical and the practical. It is concluded, looking at the general scheme, that scientific and technological activity share practically all their main elements and differ mainly in the object to which they tend, in one case the scientific model and in the other the technological product.

  

1. Interaction. The first stage corresponds to measurement in empirical terms, the interaction between the object to be measured and the measuring instrument, which is considered to come from the production stage, the last of the six stages to be analyzed in this scheme.
    
2. Computing. Then comes the symbolic stage of measurement, in which the raw data reading is computed until reaching the outcome. At this stage, mathematical knowledge is mainly involved.
    
3. Verification. With the outcome, going from the practical scope of measurement to the theoretical scope of speculation on the validity of a model, the hypothesis that gave rise to the need for measurement is confirmed or not depending on whether the data obtained falls within what is expected by following the hypothesis. If such is the case, the verification results in the confirmation of one unitary element of the model.
    
4. Project. The scientific model obtained from the hypothesis and a series of instances of verification of its unitary elements is, on the one hand, an end in itself for science, whose main aim is to know the world by turning it into nature. This does not prevent the models that science confirms from being used in technological objects construction projects, in which other so-called technological models also interact. Technological models use knowledge from scientific models, but their purpose is not to know nature but to intervene on it.
    
5. Design. After using theoretical models to project the production of a technological object, the first instance of the project is carried out with the design of such an object, for which practical models related to its design and production intervene.
    
6. Production. Once the models are ready, the factual production proceeds, moving from the symbolic domain of the model to the empirical domain. Production gives rise to a new technological object that can be used outside the scientific field. But the main interest of this scheme is to show the circular process by which scientific models give rise to the technological production of measuring instruments that science itself needs to obtain its scientific models.
    

  

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

  

According to the scheme thus explained, items b to e belong to the symbolic field, while items a and d belong to the empirical field. Likewise, items a, b, e and f belong to the practical field while items c and d to the theoretical field. Perhaps it is convenient to suggest the meaning of the terms "empirical", "symbolic", "theoretical" and "practical" from this scheme, rather than engaging in a discussion about the transcendent meanings of these words to see later if they are accurately applied to the scheme (even though it sounds very strange to carry out epistemological relations from a pragmatic criterion). The scheme can also be summarized to show two main movements. On the one hand, the theoretical-practical movement by which a project becomes a technological object. On the other hand, the empirical-symbolic movement by which a certain object comes to serve as a target for a model. The prolixity of the scheme also allows the activities to be grouped “vertically”, so that it can be said that production and interaction are both empirical-practical activities; computing and design are both symbolic-practical activities; while checking and projection are both symbolic-theoretical activities.

Items d and a show a remarkable similarity in their own symmetrical opposition within respect to the proposed scheme. Item d can be assumed as the starting point of the technological process, the moment of ideation and the model projection of a technological process, and there the diagram shows the confluence of two types of models: the properly scientific models and the technological models, which are not properly scientific but are strongly based on scientific knowledge. Therefore science in its final product is an essential part of technology at the origin of its process. Similarly, item a can be assumed as the starting point of scientific activity: the laboratory activity, the moment when the world is scrutinized to extract its secrets. At this stage, two types of objects converge, one properly technological, the measuring instrument, and the other being the object to be measured, which is strongly influenced by technology. From this it is possible to follow the nowadays current criterion proposed by Bunge (1966) according to which technology is applied science, but also suggesting that science is, in its own way, applied technology. The way in which technology is applied to science is manifested in the experiment.

This makes it possible to go one step further in the problem of demarcation, and it is clarified that taking charge of such a problem is not a choice for any account of the philosophy of science, but rather the very subject with which it must ultimately deal. In section 1.2 it had been suggested that the conceptual structure is a distinctive note of the scientific, but it was clarified that as symbolic it only attacks one half of the problem. Indeed, music theory contains a more defined and structured conceptual net than many other disciplines that are considered scientific. And why do we say that music is art instead of science? Now it can be seen that the difference is expressed by the association of science with technology. The scientific model is a product that the engineer uses to materially mold nature, which results in the production of technological unities that with a symphony as instrument it could never be achieved. This, however, is not intended to put an end to the demarcation problem, the main axis of which revolves around scientific representation, and that is why at the end of this essay it will be the promoter of additional reflections.

  
  

## 4.7 The world-nature tension expressed in the hypothesis, in the experiment and in technological production

  

Extremely exceptional are those cases in which the measurement is performed on a system that has not been technologically touched. But the fact that it has been technologically modified is not enough for it to be considered a scientific system. The object that is interesting to science is not only the one that is available to know it, but the one that science produces to therefore come to know it (Hacking 1983, ch. 13; 1992). When science technologically intervenes on an object to observe its properties, the result is what is known as a scientific experiment, which is no longer just a measurement of things that can usually be found in daily life outside the laboratory. Rather reverse the equation: the formal background of those things we usually find today outside the laboratory were once forced into existence in a laboratory experiment for the first time. With this key it is possible to read another corollary of the scientific-technological cycle studied in this section: science naturalizes the world, technology intervenes on the natural object known by science, and finally the world absorbs the technological product whose scientific foundations have been hidden for the user. There is a very interesting point of analysis in the last step, which can be called the “interface effect” of the technological object, according to which a non scientist can use a technically very complex object without knowing the vast majority of the principles of its construction. Technological objects have their usage models well differentiated from their construction models. The interface effect is precisely what allows this differentiation, and it will not be analyzed here further, mainly because its study in terms of philosophy of science is todaypractically nil.

In section 3.2 it was said, within the framework of the distinction between nature and world, that a new model rises above the everyday world, and this always offers resistance and anchors the former, so that, in order to transcend the community, the proposed model cannot mark an excessive distance with this knowledge. Now, in view of the recent discussion, it is noted that the daily knowledge is in turn in many ways influenced by technical knowledge, either because many scientific concepts and worldviews according to scientific models end up becoming over time in part of the cultural baggage of the society and they are taught, for example, in regular schools, either because technological products, always built at least in part based on scientific models, also become common currency. This allows to speak of a kind of feedback in which science has as a daily anchor for its development, but this at its time is in turn historically being modified in the direction in which science has advanced, so that the successive new scientific models start from an increasingly technical soil, and it is assumed that consequently they will be able to go further in their proposal in comparison to more "precarious" models whose hypotheses emerge from non/less-technical knowledge.

But there is a second consideration to understand why science has an even longer string than that suggested by its direct relationship with the non-technical world to trace the kite of its speculation, and this extension is related to the interface of the technological instrument. The possibility of covering from the user the scientific foundations of a technological object allows the engineer to evade the limit of the user's knowledge for its use. If it is accepted, as suggested in section 3.2, that it is a condition for the acceptance of a model that it is applicable at least potentially, it should be noted that the problem of applicability, and therefore that of the acceptance of a scientific model resides largely in the ability of engineers to design a technological object whose interfaces allows it to convert the technical use of the sum of parts to the daily use of the object as a whole. This, well read, means that when evaluating a scientific model, the community is obliged to consider its applicability as potential—since for the design of technological objects based on a scientific model, the model must already be available—but only when this applicability becomes a matter of fact (this has historically been the case each time) the models are fully accepted (here still following Hacking 1992). And this has a very powerful reason: that for the production of a technological object it is necessary to repeat with high precision what science did in the laboratory for the first time, so the production of technological objects is proof of the accuracy of the scientific model adopted by the engineer that no one can deny.

To the effort of imagination that the scientist or creator of a model must make in semantic terms to convert part of everyday language into technical language and thus contribute to the knowledge of nature it is added, as condition for the full acceptance of the model, the design effort of engineers to ideate an object that conceals its fundamentals to the user. In between these two, a third effort of imagination must still be added, which is certainly in the very limit between the scientific and the technological, which consists in the design of the contrastation experiment by which the model must begin to consider itself accepted. These three efforts of imagination that coordinate with each other according to the stage of confirmation in which the model is, are three aspects of the tension between the world and nature that has been introduced in section 3. It is not superfluous to clarify that, for each of these three stages listed, the world-nature tension manifests itself in the novel aspect each time, not in the other unitary elements that the model already takes from the available natural knowledge, with a markedly lower level of effort and controversy.

The scientific experiment has its center of gravity in a measurement event and in a measurement system, but certainly it is not considered an experiment to that measurement that is carried out without in any way tensioning the object being measured. This is the essential meaning of the term "laboratory": that context that allows controlled modification of the object to be measured. How far can science go in this context modification to make its measurement? Assuming that it is not a situation in which the context is modified for the sole purpose of observing what happens, but that the modification is guided by a hypothesis, then an idea of ​​such distance will be given by the hypothesis. But the most forceful benchmark will be given by the technology available for the time, and this is also the main factor that the hypothesis must consider: it can rise only to a certain extent in speculation over the available contrast capacity, and in the case of such excess it will have to wait for the technology to develop so that it can be contrasted, being unable in the meantime to do more than devise imaginary experiments—which are themselves an institution and their general meaning is none other than that: to be lawful devices to imagine a measurement situation when the technology to carry out such measurement is not available.

  

# 6. Scientific representation based on the equivalence relationship between the respective patterns of the model and the target

According to this, it would be a methodological fail to say something like "X is a representation of Y iff..." when asking about representation, because in this case "representation" is merely replacing "model", and although it is not possible to speak of an error strictly, it falls into the recklessness of explaining what a model is mistakenly believing that representation is being explained. Therefore the representation itself, which is what the model performs in relation to its target, remains unexplained no matter how complete the solution to the problem thus posed has been. …

Formalizing as isomorphic the relationship between the model and its target, understanding scientific representation as a mathematical function, should not be a direct and caution-free step. The first indication is that the relationship between the target and the model does not need to become a function, since the point of interest is the equivalence relationship between their respective patterns, of which it has been said in section 1.4 above that it is not appropriate to be considered as a representation. Rather, both patterns must be equivalent so that the material correlative systems in which they are embedded can give rise to representation.

Thus, due to the equivalence between both patterns, the corresponding function is the identity function. This reflects the simplicity of the isomorphic relationship, but brings a complication with the following question, which would not be difficult to tackle if the relationship were not symmetrical: which of the patterns should be considered the domain and which the codomain fur such function? Is the model pattern a function of the target pattern or vice versa? In all the cases studied from this point of view, there seems to have been no complication in assuming, without prior discussion, the model as the function that represents its target. But in section 2 it has been said that the model is not something that emerges as a function of the natural system it represents, but rather the natural system is what emerges from the world from its representation by a model. Therefore, this natural system is a function of the model and not vice versa.

~~The model pattern is by design a complete and homogeneous system while the target pattern is always necessarily divided into two subgroups: on the one hand, the subgroup of the unitary elements that have been already checked, which will always have an inaccurate value due to the measurement uncertainty. On the other hand, the subgroup of the elements that have not been checked and are considered part of the natural system only for consistency with respect to the other elements according to what the model projects, so they are elements in some sense potential. Both subgroups could not be considered in mathematical terms if they were part of the domain. How could a value in the codomain be represented from a value in the domain that is either only possible or inaccurate? Being part of the codomain, on the other hand, a second function that modifies the resulting value of the first function is sufficient, as will be seen next. Note that this shift in the relationship between domain and codomain for the isomorphic function is a direct and immediate consequence of the shift in the realistic conception presented in the section 3.3.~~

  

A view that can be understood free of this warning is one that takes the models as set-theoretical structures. Even the account presented here could be thought of as very close to this view. In fact, the pattern that constitutes the formal nucleus of any model is a structure that can be thought of as isomorphic in relation to that of the target pattern, and the function that relates them is the identity function. Certainly, it would be an embedded isomorphism (...), i.e. embedded in the material model of the case. But is this the case actually? To consider it in such terms, there must be a function 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 such that 𝑓(𝑥)=x where the domain X is embedded in the model and the codomain Y is embedded in the target. Here a series of adjustments must be made so that this function corresponds to the formal relationship between the respective patterns, since it has been admitted that the respective patterns do not coincide completely but only partially, and their coincidence increases as a possibility, this increase being the objective of the scientific normal activity itself.

There is a lot of juggling to put this in formal terms. It can be thought that there is a subset P of the codomain with elements that are only possible, not actually existing [checked?]. This could be thought of as a second function 𝑔:𝑋→𝑌 so that 𝑔(𝑥) is opaque in some sense for 𝑓(𝑥)∈P. That it is opaque could be formalized by taking that its elements have an associated possibility that goes from 0 to 1. Thus, it can be consider a binary operation 𝑔∘𝑓 such that 𝑔(𝑥) associates the elements of 𝑓(𝑥)∈P by a number that it goes from 0 to 1 according to a given distribution. This “association” is not a multiplication, since the actual value of each element (if it has a numerical value) does not change.

To this it must be added that for those elements actually existing in the target, e.i. for 𝑓(𝑥)∉P the identity prescribed by the function 𝑓(𝑥) is not always in general but approximate (pace the uncertainty in measurement). This could be formalized assuming that the function 𝑔(𝑥) is noisy (in some sense) for 𝑓(𝑥)∉P, this is, it multiplies each element of 𝑓(𝑥)∉P by a number close to 1 according to a given distribution.

All this can be considered correct only after assuming that some factors cannot be determined in general terms, but depend on the model in question each time, and even on the current state of the model in question:

  

- As explained in section 1.4 above, the range of subset P cannot be determined with any formula. [esta parece ser la única que queda con fuerza]
    
- The "opacity" of the elements of 𝑔(𝑥) cannot be determined a priori either. That is, the value between 0 and 1 by which each element of 𝑓(𝑥)∈P is by principle unknown in general terms. [se podría resolver con sucesivas contrastaciones, si es necesario]
    
- The "noise" of 𝑔(𝑥) also cannot be formally determined. The value for each element will tend to be closer to 1 according to an asymptotic curve for which a function cannot be established in principle. [esto no tiene que ver con la incertidumbre de la medición?]
    

  

Given these caveats, does it still make sense to bet on formalization to explain scientific models? Is there something lost if this notation stops being used? Does it even provide clarity in any sense? Can it help in any way to reach consensus as to what a scientific model is?

  

The question of whether this account can be defined as structuralist will remain as undefined as the question of whether it can do without structure.

  

In their great generality, structuralist accounts demand a "reconstruction" of current scientific theories with a structuralist key. In this account, the nuances given to the description of the structure lead to reconciliation with scientific practice as it has been occurring, and as a consequence it does not require, by method, any meta-theoretical condiment to knowledge as published in Journals, as presented at conferences and as exposed in class at all levels.


# Final comments


One reason the representation problem in ontological terms is not further analyzed here is that it refers to representation in general and not just to representation in science. Depending on how it is handled, it can even cover the vast semantic problem of oral and written language, according to which a word designates a thing in most general terms. Thus understood, it becomes an endless analysis, more considering the limits of the present work, which on the other hand does not need for its approach more than the clarification of the problem of representation in science in epistemic terms, and this is intended to have been adequately achieved. Every scientist is empowered to rest, in epistemic terms, on the formula "one is one", which means "every unitary element in the model claims to have its equivalent unitary element in the target". The formula is directly understandable and has functioned underground since science is science, despite the fact that the meaning of "is" in said formula is always indefinite.
  

Any two things can be thought of that have absolutely nothing to do with each other, and yet both coincide in that they are "things". Similarly, the unity of science does not consist in establishing the need to achieve a net that connects all the models that are presumed to be scientific so that the demarcation between what is science and what is not is reduced to a single though complex boundary. Rather, herein it is claimed to have shown that there is nothing to be achieved in this sense, not even to be understood, but rather to expose what has always been considered, that scientific models, however different they may be each other, they are scientific because they consist of conceptual systems, and thus the unity of science is reduced to the simplicity of scientific unity.

An enormous attempt has been made to show that to distinguish what is commonly called science it may be misguided to raise a model attached to science with formal or mathematical language, but rather to point out what in fact operates and has operated there whenever a knowledge system was called scientific: the conceptual unity. For this, the path has been forced to go to what is congenital to conceptual knowledge, which is representation. And the representation in turn guided the scientific element that concentrates its main components, the measuring instrument, in its very structure. The analysis of the measuring instrument led to the standard unit, which ended up becoming the foundation for the reliable establishment of any unitary system, with which it was intended to close the argumentative circle. Now the reader can judge whether the attempt has been neat and adequate enough to warrant further attention.
